title: Thanks, and let it be
line: Seven evenings: a minute of gratitude, and one ἔστω.
intro: Athena ends lessons with gratitude: εὐχαριστία, from εὖ, well, and χάρις, grace, activates grace, the incalculable factor that completes eudaimonia together with our own effort. For what is hard, Athena offers a mathematician’s tool: ἔστω, “let it be so”, the word a proof begins with. For seven evenings, close the day with a minute of each.
does: Each evening, a minute of gratitude, then one thing from the day that you let be.
trains: Gratitude that opens you to grace, and acceptance that loosens resistance.

each.title: Gratitude
each.text: Take one minute this evening and name what you are grateful for today. Pair it with your own effort, as the old proverb says: “with Athena (the goddess), move your hand too”.

each.title: Let it be
each.text: Then take one thing from the day that you resisted, starting with small ones (a delay, a remark, a plan that fell through), and say ἔστω, “let it be”: as a working hypothesis, let it be perfect and just, happening for a reason you cannot see from partway up the mountain. Then let it go.

note: What were you grateful for today?
end: After seven evenings: what has gratitude changed in how your days close, and what has become easier to let be?
